newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon seeks minimal force cuts, base closings.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon seeks minimal force cuts, base closings.

text.p: Marching into a political minefield, the U.S. Defense Department on Monday asked Congress to close more military bases but make only small troop cuts while spending billions on arms to build a force for the 21st century.

Defense Secretary William Cohen unveiled the plan, pressing reluctant lawmakers to authorize two rounds of new domestic base closings in 1999 and 2001 to save money for stealth jets and other weapons while cutting only 61,700 troops from the 1.4 million-member military.

The Quadrennial Defense Review, or "QDR" as the proposal is known, has drawn criticism from Democrats and Republicans in Congress because it seeks sensitive base closings but would cancel virtually no big arms programs.

The review plan, which requires Congressional approval, would retain the current total of about 100,000 American troops in both Europe and the Western Pacific and keep the military prepared to fight two wars virtually at once, for example in the Middle East and Korea.

"The flush of euphoria (after the Cold War), must be tempered with the knowledge that while the prospect of horrific, global war has receded, new threats and dangers ... have gathered on the horizon," Cohen said in the report.

The most controversial issue is bases. Closings are an explosive matter in communities that depend on local military paychecks, especially after Congress has closed 98 major domestic facilities in four previous rounds.
Cohen has told lawmakers that the United States has too many bases now that the armed forces have already been cut by one-third since the end of the Cold War.

The plan would make some reductions in Air Force F-22 "stealth" fighters being developed by Lockheed Martin Corp., Navy FA-18E/F fighters built McDonnell Douglas Corp. and Marine Corps' V-22 tilt-rotor helicopters being built by Boeing Co. and the Bell Helicopter division of Textron Inc..

But it would not cancel any of those multibillion-dollar programs and would retain long-range plans for a $170 billion joint strike fighter program that Lockheed Martin and Boeing are competing to build in the next century.
"I'm very disappointed," said Republican Rep. Curt Weldon of Pennsylvania as the plan was released. "It does not get at the heart of the issue, which is the need to cut some major weapons programs.
"This doesn't do that. It simply slides programs to the out years and raises the cost," Weldon added in an interview on CNN as the plan was sent to Capitol Hill.

In addition to the small active-duty force cut of 61,700, the proposal would cut 54,000 troops from part-time reserve and National Guard forces, 45,000 of those from the Army, another touchy issue with lawmakers.
Many cities and towns in the United States have reserve units, and the part-time troops depend on their paychecks for supplemental income.
Of the active-duty cuts proposed by Cohen, the Air Force would take the biggest slice with 26,900. The Navy would be reduced by 18,000, the Army by 15,000 and the Marine Corps by 1,800.
The proposal also recommended that 70,000 civilian jobs be cut from the armed forces' support network and predicted that even deeper cuts will be made in the bureaucracy following further studies.

But the Air Force, Navy and Marines would benefit from retention of their major fighter jet and aircraft programs for the 21st Century -- the radar-avoiding F-22, the FA-18E/F and the V-22 tilt-rotor helicopter, which takes off and lands like a helicopter but flies like a fixed-wing plane.
The Air Force's previously planned purchase of 438 F-22s would be reduced to 339. The cost of that program under the full buy had been estimated at about $67 billion.
Cohen recommended that the Navy buy between 548 and 785 FA-18E/Fs. The Navy had planned to buy 1,000 of the aircraft for about $80 billion by 2015.
The V-22 would be reduced from 425 to 360. But procurement would be speeded up to address urgent Marine assault needs.
